analogy.p: Imagine pushing a door. If you push right next to the hinge the door barely moves, but if you push at the handle, on the far edge, the same push swings it open easily. The hinge is the pivot, the push is the force, and the distance from the hinge to your hand is the distance in M = F d: further away means a bigger moment. Two people pushing on opposite sides of the door can hold it still when their moments are equal, which is the principle of moments. The analogy breaks down because a door can only turn about one fixed line, while many pivots in physics problems, such as a seesaw balanced in different places, can be chosen anywhere, and a real door also has friction at the hinge.

bullets: A **moment** is the turning effect of a force about a pivot.
The pivot is the point about which the object turns (the hinge of a door, the bolt under a spanner, the middle of a seesaw).
A moment can be **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**, depending on the way the force tries to turn the object.
The moment depends on **two things**: the size of the force and how far from the pivot the force acts.
A force acting **through** the pivot has a distance of zero, so it has **no moment** and cannot turn the object.
Everyday examples: pushing a door close to the hinge is hard because the distance is small; a long-handled spanner or a long lever gives a big moment for the same force.
This topic is **Physics only (triple science)** in the AQA specification, in the forces topic.
Link to forces: a moment is created by a force, so the unit of the force (N) appears in the unit of the moment (N m).
core.h: Turning effects: what a moment is
core.p: A force can make an object **move in a line**, but if the force acts at a distance from a **pivot** (a fixed point the object can turn about) it can also make the object **rotate**. The turning effect of a force is called its **moment**. A big moment is what lets you undo a tight nut with a long spanner or open a heavy door by pushing on the handle rather than near the hinge. Moments are the rotational equivalent of force, and the idea is used in levers, gears, seesaws, cranes and balances.

bullets: Equation in words: **moment (newton-metre, N m) = force (newton, N) x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (metre, m)**.
Symbols: **M = F d**. Rearranged: **F = M / d** and **d = M / F**.
Units: the unit of moment is the **newton-metre (N m)**. Do not confuse it with the joule (J): although both are N m, a moment is a turning effect, not an energy.
Convert distances in cm to m before calculating: 25 cm = 0.25 m.
Doubling the force doubles the moment; doubling the distance also doubles the moment.
To get the same moment with a smaller force, apply the force **further from the pivot**.
If a force is applied at an angle, the perpendicular distance is smaller, so the moment is smaller: the best way to turn something is to push at **right angles** to the lever.
Example: a force of 40 N applied 0.25 m from a bolt gives a moment of 40 x 0.25 = 10 N m.
core.h: The equation for the moment of a force
core.p: The size of the moment is given by **moment of a force (N m) = force (N) x distance (m)**, written **M = F d**. The distance is the **perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force**. The 'line of action' is the straight line along which the force acts, extended both ways. If the force is not at right angles to the lever, the effective distance is the shortest (perpendicular) distance from the pivot to that line, not the length of the lever itself.

bullets: The **line of action** is the line the force acts along, drawn through the point where the force is applied, in the direction of the force.
The **perpendicular distance** is the shortest distance from the pivot to this line, and it meets the line at 90 degrees.
If the force acts along a line that passes through the pivot, the perpendicular distance is **zero** and the moment is **zero**.
For a vertical weight on a horizontal beam, the distance is simply the horizontal distance from the pivot to where the weight hangs.
For a weight hanging from a string, the line of action is the line of the string, even if the object is hanging at an angle to the beam.
A common exam diagram shows a force at an angle: use the perpendicular distance given or drawn, not the slanted length.
The weight of a uniform object acts through its **centre of mass** (the middle of a uniform plank), so for a uniform beam use half the length as the distance when the pivot is at one end.
Draw the line of action as a dashed line and the perpendicular as a short right-angled line to check your distance.
core.h: Perpendicular distance and the line of action
core.p: The most common mistake with moments is measuring the wrong distance. The distance in M = F d must be measured **at right angles to the line of action of the force**, from the pivot. If the force is vertical, measure the horizontal distance to the pivot; if the force is horizontal, measure the vertical distance. This is why pushing a door at an angle is less effective than pushing straight at it, and why a spanner works best when you pull at 90 degrees to the handle.

bullets: **Principle of moments**: for a balanced object, **sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments** (about the same pivot).
If clockwise moments are bigger, the object turns clockwise; if anticlockwise moments are bigger it turns anticlockwise.
Method: choose the pivot; for each force, work out F x d; sort into clockwise and anticlockwise; add each group; set them equal.
A force on the right of the pivot pushing down gives a clockwise moment; a force on the left of the pivot pushing down gives an anticlockwise moment.
For several forces on one side, **add** their moments together before equating.
The balance of moments is separate from the balance of forces: a balanced seesaw also has an upward force at the pivot equal to the total downward weight.
Worked pattern: 300 N at 2.0 m on the left (anticlockwise 600 N m) balances 400 N at 1.5 m on the right (clockwise 600 N m).
This is the same idea that makes a see-saw balance with a light child far from the pivot and a heavy child close to it.
core.h: Clockwise and anticlockwise moments: the principle of moments
core.p: If an object is **balanced** (in equilibrium, not turning), then the **total clockwise moment about any pivot is equal to the total anticlockwise moment** about that same pivot. This is the **principle of moments**. It is used to find an unknown force or distance on a seesaw, a balance, a crane or a lever. Each force that tries to turn the object clockwise has a moment, and each that tries to turn it anticlockwise has a moment, and for balance the two totals must be equal.

bullets: For a lever in balance: **effort x distance of effort from pivot = load x distance of load from pivot**.
**To lift a heavy load with a small force**, put the effort **far from the pivot** and the load **close to the pivot** (a long crowbar, a wheelbarrow with long handles, a long spanner).

There are three arrangements: pivot in the middle (seesaw, crowbar, scissors), load in the middle (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener), effort in the middle (tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm).
In the first two arrangements the lever is a **force multiplier** (the effort is smaller than the load) because the effort arm is longer than the load arm.
When the effort is in the middle (tweezers) the effort is larger than the load, but the lever gives a larger **movement** and finer control.
A lever does not create energy: the work done by the effort equals the work done on the load (ignoring losses), which is why the longer-arm effort moves further.
Explaining a lever in an exam: 'the force is applied further from the pivot, so the moment is greater for the same force, so less force is needed.'
Wheelbarrow example: load 300 N, 0.6 m from the wheel; handles 1.2 m from the wheel; effort = 300 x 0.6 / 1.2 = 150 N.
core.h: Levers: how a lever transmits a turning effect
core.p: A **lever** is a rigid bar that can turn about a pivot. It transmits the **rotational effect** of a force: you apply an **effort** at one point, and the lever applies a **force** (the load) at another point. Because the moment of the effort is effort x its distance from the pivot, a long distance from the pivot lets a small effort balance or overcome a large load that is close to the pivot. A lever therefore makes a task easier by letting you use a **smaller force**, although you must move the effort through a **larger distance**.

bullets: Two meshed gears turn in **opposite directions**: if one turns clockwise, the other turns anticlockwise.
The **contact force** between the teeth is the same size on both gears (Newton's third law), but the moment depends on the force x the radius of the gear.
A **larger gear** has a greater radius, so the same force at its teeth gives a **bigger moment**: the larger gear delivers more turning effect and turns **more slowly**.
A **smaller gear** turns **faster** (it has fewer teeth to pass the same number of teeth) but delivers a smaller moment.
Gear teeth count: when two gears mesh, the same number of teeth pass the contact point on each. A gear with twice the teeth turns at half the speed, as a rule.
A car gearbox uses different gear pairs: low gears give a big moment at the wheels for starting off or climbing, high gears give high speed.
A **gear train** can be used to transmit rotation between axles that are some distance apart, and to reverse the direction if needed.
Gear teeth must be in contact: to keep the direction the same, a third (idler) gear can be placed between them, which changes direction twice.
core.p: A **gear** is a wheel with teeth around its edge. When two gears **mesh** (their teeth interlock), turning one gear makes the other turn. The force from the teeth of the first gear on the teeth of the second gives a **moment** that turns the second gear. Gears transmit the **rotational effect of a force** from one axle to another, and they can change the size of the moment, the speed of rotation and the direction of rotation.

bullets: Rule for speeds: **number of teeth on A x speed of A = number of teeth on B x speed of B**, so the bigger gear (more teeth) turns slower.
Rule for moments: a gear with twice the radius (and twice the teeth) receives twice the moment, if the force between the teeth is the same.
Example: A has 20 teeth and turns at 60 revolutions per minute; B has 40 teeth, so B turns at 20 x 60 / 40 = 30 rev/min in the opposite direction.
Example of the trade-off: bicycle gears. A low gear (large rear gear) makes pedalling easier (a bigger moment on the wheel) but the bike goes slower for each pedal turn.
Do not say 'a bigger gear makes it faster': a bigger gear turns more slowly but provides more moment.
Gear ratio is not usually asked as a formula in GCSE papers, but you should be able to **compare** two gears and say which turns faster or gives a bigger moment.
Gear wheels are often made of metals such as steel for strength; teeth are lubricated to reduce friction and wear (link to friction).
The force and moment are 'transmitted' because the first gear exerts a force on the second, which creates a moment on the second gear's axle.
core.h: Comparing gears: size, speed and moment
core.p: For two meshing gears A and B, the number of teeth passing the contact point per second is the same. So **(teeth on A) x (rotation rate of A) = (teeth on B) x (rotation rate of B)**. A gear with more teeth turns more slowly. The moment transmitted is greater for the larger gear because the force at the teeth acts at a bigger radius. This is a trade-off: a gear pair can give a bigger moment or a bigger speed, not both. The ratio of the tooth counts tells you the ratio of the speeds (inverse) and of the moments (direct).

bullets: Step 1: Draw or label the pivot and the forces. Mark the distances from the pivot, in metres.
Step 2: Work out each moment M = F d, with units N m.
Step 3: Sort the moments into clockwise and anticlockwise.
Step 4: Write 'total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment' (principle of moments).
Step 5: Rearrange to find the unknown force or distance, and give the unit.
If the pivot is at one end, the weight of a uniform plank acts at the **centre of the plank** (half its length from the pivot).
Check your answer: the larger distance should go with the smaller force.
If the beam is not balanced, the larger total moment shows the direction in which it will turn.
core.h: Worked reasoning: using moments to find unknown forces or distances
core.p: Most moment calculations follow a repeatable recipe. First identify the pivot. Second list every force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot. Third decide whether each moment is clockwise or anticlockwise. Fourth add up each direction and set the totals equal if the object is balanced. Finally rearrange to find the unknown. Showing each step makes it easy for the examiner to award method marks even if you make an arithmetic slip.

bullets: **Seesaw**: a lighter person sits further from the pivot, the heavier person closer, so the moments balance.
**Spanner**: a longer spanner increases the distance, increasing the moment for the same force, which loosens a tight nut.
**Door**: the handle is at the opposite edge from the hinge for the largest distance; pushing near the hinge needs a very large force.
**Crane**: the counterweight and load are placed so that the clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the tower balance; if the load moves further out, the moment increases and the crane could tip.
**Wheelbarrow**: the wheel is the pivot; the long handles give a big distance for the effort.
**Wrench versus screwdriver**: a thick handle gives a larger radius over which your hand applies force, so a larger moment.
**Human body**: the forearm acts as a lever with the elbow as the pivot; the biceps pulls close to the pivot so a large muscle force lifts a small load.
**Safety**: tall objects topple when the moment of their weight about the edge exceeds the restoring moment, which is why low centres of mass make things stable.
core.h: Moments in the real world: seesaws, spanners, doors and cranes
core.p: Moments explain how many everyday and engineering devices work. A balanced seesaw works because the moments are equal; a spanner or wrench makes use of a long handle so that a small force gives a big moment; a door handle is placed far from the hinges to maximise the moment. A tower crane has a counterweight on the short arm to balance the moment of the load on the long arm, so it does not topple. In each case the principle of moments tells us how large the forces or distances must be.

bullets: Equilibrium needs **no resultant force** (so no acceleration) and **no resultant moment** (so no turning).
At a pivot there is a **reaction force** upwards equal in size to the total downward force when the beam is horizontal and balanced.
A moment acting on its own would make an object rotate with increasing speed; moments are the 'turning' version of Newton's second law.
The weight of an object acts through its centre of mass; if a support is under the centre of mass the object is balanced without turning.
Moments in a lever can be used to find the force at the pivot: reaction = load + effort (for the balanced cases where both act downwards).
Link to energy: levers and gears do not give you more energy; the work done at the input equals the work output (less wasted energy due to friction).
Link to work: a smaller force over a bigger distance can do the same work as a bigger force over a smaller distance.
Link to the required knowledge of vector quantities: forces have size and direction; the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) matters for a moment.
core.h: Rotation, equilibrium and links to other forces ideas
core.p: An object is in **equilibrium** when it is neither accelerating nor turning, which requires both the **resultant force to be zero** and the **resultant moment to be zero**. At GCSE you mainly use the principle of moments, but you should link it to the idea that a balanced object has forces in balance too. For a seesaw, the upward force at the pivot (the reaction) equals the sum of the downward forces, which is what stops it moving vertically.

bullets: If the force is applied at an angle to a lever, the **perpendicular distance decreases**, so the **moment decreases** for the same force. To keep the same moment you need a bigger force.
If you double the distance and halve the force, the moment is unchanged: M = F d stays the same.
A gear system exchanging speed for moment: this is similar to a lever exchanging force for distance moved. In both cases there is a trade-off.
Design question: why is a bicycle spanner long and a watchmaker's screwdriver thin? A long handle gives a large moment from a small force; a thin screwdriver needs small moments and fine control.
Evaluate: levers make work easier but do not reduce the work needed; friction at the pivot wastes some energy as heat.
If a beam is not uniform, the weight acts at the centre of mass, which may not be in the middle.
Link to Newton's third law: the pair of forces between meshed teeth are equal and opposite, which is why the gears move in opposite directions.
Link to friction and lubrication: oil on a pivot or on gear teeth reduces friction and so reduces wasted energy and wear.
core.h: Higher-tier thinking: explaining and evaluating moments, levers and gears
core.p: The top-grade answers use precise language: they refer to the **perpendicular distance from the pivot**, to the **line of action**, and to the **principle of moments**, and they explain a design choice in terms of moments (for example why a handle is long). You should also be able to compare designs (a long spanner versus a short one), predict what happens when a distance or force is changed, and say how the moment changes if the force is applied at an angle.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark)**: 'moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot', or 'N m'. Quote the equation exactly and include the word perpendicular.
**Calculate a moment (2 to 3 marks)**: equation (1), correct substitution in metres (1), answer with N m (1).
**Use the principle of moments (3 to 4 marks)**: calculate each moment (1 each), state clockwise total = anticlockwise total (1), rearrange to find the unknown with a unit (1).
**Explain how a lever makes a job easier (2 to 3 marks)**: 'the force is applied further from the pivot (1), so the moment is greater for the same force (1), so a smaller force is needed (1)'.
**Explain how gears work (3 marks)**: the teeth mesh and one gear exerts a force on the other (1), which gives a moment that turns it (1), in the opposite direction (1).
**Compare two gears (2 to 3 marks)**: bigger gear has more teeth, turns more slowly, and gives a larger moment; smaller gear turns faster.
**Diagram questions**: mark the pivot, forces and perpendicular distances; for balanced beams label clockwise and anticlockwise.
**Units**: convert to metres; give moments in N m. Check answers are sensible (for example, the lighter person sits further away).
**6 mark questions**: describe how to use a lever or balance a beam in sequence, using the equation, the principle of moments, a worked example and a conclusion.
**Command words**: 'Calculate' requires working and units; 'Explain' requires reasons using the idea of moments; 'Describe' states what happens.

mistakes.r: Moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
mistakes.w: Using the length of the lever instead of the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action.

mistakes.r: Convert cm to m (divide by 100) before using M = F d. The unit is N m.
mistakes.w: Leaving distances in cm and getting the wrong moment.

mistakes.r: Add all clockwise moments together and all anticlockwise moments together, then equate.
mistakes.w: Calculating only one side and forgetting to add multiple moments on the same side.

mistakes.r: A balanced object needs the clockwise moments to equal the anticlockwise moments: use the principle of moments.
mistakes.w: Saying 'the forces are balanced so the seesaw is balanced'.

mistakes.r: A bigger gear (more teeth) turns more slowly but transmits a bigger moment; meshed gears turn in opposite directions.
mistakes.w: Saying a bigger gear turns faster.

mistakes.r: The unit of moment is the newton-metre (N m); do not call it joules.
mistakes.w: Writing the unit of moment as N or J.

mistakes.r: A lever lets a smaller force do the job over a larger distance; the work done is the same (apart from losses).
mistakes.w: Saying a lever 'gives you extra energy' or 'does less work'.

mistakes.r: A long handle increases the distance, so the moment is bigger for the same force.
mistakes.w: Saying 'a long handle means more force'.

mistakes.r: Use the centre of mass of a uniform beam (half its length) as the position of its weight.
mistakes.w: Forgetting that the weight of a uniform beam acts at its centre.

summary: The specification (Physics only) asks you to recall and use the equation moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action (M = F d), to apply the principle of moments to balanced objects, and to explain how levers and gears transmit the rotational effects of forces. It matters because moments explain how spanners, seesaws, cranes, bicycles and gearboxes work, and it is a common source of calculation and explanation marks.

terms.d: The turning effect of a force about a pivot; moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
The fixed point about which an object can turn.
The unit of the moment of a force: one newton acting at a perpendicular distance of one metre.
The straight line along which a force acts, passing through the point where the force is applied.
The shortest distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, measured at 90 degrees to that line.
A moment that tends to turn an object in the same direction as the hands of a clock.
A moment that tends to turn an object in the opposite direction to the hands of a clock.
For an object in equilibrium (balanced), the total clockwise moment about a pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about the same pivot.
The state in which an object is not accelerating or turning because the resultant force and the resultant moment are both zero.
A rigid bar that turns about a pivot and transmits the rotational effect of a force, allowing a small force to balance or move a larger one.
The force applied to a lever or machine to move the load.
The force that a lever has to overcome or lift.
A toothed wheel that meshes with another to transmit the rotational effect of a force from one axle to another.
The interlocking of the teeth of two gears so that turning one causes the other to turn.
The point through which the weight of an object appears to act; the middle of a uniform object.
A device such as a lever that allows a larger force to be exerted on a load than the effort applied.
The force exerted by the pivot or support on an object, balancing the downward forces.
The tendency of a force to cause turning about a pivot.

worked.ans: (a) 10 N m; (b) 20 N. Doubling the distance halves the force needed for the same moment.
worked.q: A mechanic uses a spanner of length 0.25 m and applies a force of 40 N at right angles to the end of the handle. (a) Calculate the moment. (b) The mechanic changes to a spanner 0.50 m long and wants the same moment. Calculate the force needed. [4 marks]
steps: Same moment with d = 0.50 m: F = M / d (1 mark).

worked.ans: 1.5 m from the pivot, on the right-hand side.
worked.q: A uniform plank is balanced on a pivot in its centre. A child of weight 300 N sits 2.0 m to the left of the pivot. A second child of weight 400 N sits on the right. Calculate the distance of the second child from the pivot. [4 marks]
steps: Anticlockwise moment = 300 x 2.0 = 600 N m (1 mark).
Balanced, so clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment = 600 N m (1 mark).

worked.ans: B turns anticlockwise at 30 rev/min; the bigger gear transmits a larger moment but turns more slowly.
worked.q: Gear A has 20 teeth and is turning clockwise at 60 revolutions per minute. It meshes with gear B, which has 40 teeth. (a) State the direction in which B turns. (b) Calculate the speed of B. (c) Explain why B can give a bigger turning effect. [5 marks]
steps: Meshed gears turn in opposite directions, so B turns anticlockwise (1 mark).
The same number of teeth pass the contact point per minute: 20 x 60 = 1200 teeth per minute (1 mark).
Speed of B = 1200 / 40 = 30 revolutions per minute (1 mark).
B is larger, so the force from the teeth of A acts at a greater radius (1 mark).
So the moment on B is greater (M = F d), although B turns more slowly (1 mark).
